suggestions.title: North by Northwest
suggestions.description: Eva Marie Saint died on Monday at 102, and this is the film to watch her in. Your shelf has met Hitchcock twice: Psycho, which is horror, and Rear Window, which is the guilt of watching. This is the third and the lightest, the only film he ever called fun, and the blueprint for everything that came after it - the wrong-man chase, the cool blonde, a set piece every nine minutes. Ernest Lehman wrote it to Hitchcock's brief ('I want to do a chase across America'), Bernard Herrmann scored it with a fandango that starts in the first frame and never quite stops, and Robert Burks shot it in VistaVision. Cary Grant is Roger O. Thornhill, an advertising man mistaken for a government agent who does not exist - the initials R.O.T. and the running joke that the O stands for nothing are the entire MacGuffin philosophy compressed into one gag. James Mason is Phillip Vandamm, Martin Landau his cold-eyed Leonard, Jessie Royce Landis (eight years older than Grant) plays his mother, and Leo G. Carroll is the Professor who started it all. The set pieces are why it sits on every list: the murder in the United Nations lobby, shot with hidden cameras because this is the only film ever given access to the General Assembly hall; the crop-duster at Prairie Stop, nine minutes of a man standing alone in a cornfield waiting for something that never arrives, with no music and almost no dialogue, which may be the most famous nothing in cinema; and the Mount Rushmore finale, built as a replica at MGM because the National Park Service refused permission. 136 minutes, three Academy Award nominations - screenplay, art direction, film editing - and it won none of them, which is the other thing worth knowing about Hitchcock: he never won a competitive Oscar in his life. IMDb 8.3.

suggestions.title: Once Upon a Time in America
suggestions.description: Sergio Leone spent about fifteen years and four aborted attempts trying to make this, and it is the last film he ever finished. It comes from Harry Grey's 1952 novel The Hoods - Grey was a pseudonym, the man claimed to have been a real New York gangster, and he met Leone once and asked him why anyone would want to make a film about a bunch of bums. The structure is the point: Noodles (Robert De Niro) is remembering, from an opium den in 1933, forty years of his life on the Lower East Side - the boys of 1921, the gangsters of 1933, the men of 1968 - and the film never tells you how much of the last act is actually happening and how much is a dying man's wish. Around De Niro: James Woods as Max, Elizabeth McGovern as Deborah, Tuesday Weld as Carol, Joe Pesci as Frankie, Danny Aiello, Burt Young, Treat Williams, William Forsythe, and James Hayden as Patsy - Hayden died of an overdose in 1983, before the film was released, so he never saw himself in it. Ennio Morricone wrote the score before shooting and Leone played it on set as he had on Once Upon a Time in the West; Deborah's Theme, on Gheorghe Zamfir's pan flute, is the best thing either man ever did. The 229-minute version took a fifteen-minute standing ovation at Cannes in May 1984. The American distributor, The Ladd Company, then cut it to 139 minutes and reordered it chronologically without Leone's involvement, and the reviews destroyed it; Roger Ebert was one of the few American critics who defended it. Leone never directed again and died in 1989. In 2012 a 251-minute cut, with twenty-five minutes nobody had seen, was restored and shown at Cannes. Your gangster spine is Goodfellas, The Godfather I and II, The Departed, Heat, The Usual Suspects - this is the big one still missing, and it is about friendship, time and memory rather than money, which is why it is the saddest film on this list. Watch the long version or none. IMDb 8.3.

suggestions.title: Finding Nemo
suggestions.description: Your animation shelf is already the strongest part of this list - Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro, Grave of the Fireflies, WALL-E, Toy Story 1 and 3, Inside Out, Spider-Verse - and this is the biggest thing missing from it. Pixar's fifth feature, and the one that made the studio untouchable: $94 million in, $940.3 million out, the highest-grossing animated film ever until Toy Story 3 took the title from it in 2010, and still the best-selling DVD of all time at over forty million copies. Andrew Stanton directed with Lee Unkrich and wrote it with Bob Peterson and David Reynolds, starting from his own fear of the ocean: he learned to dive, the crew studied reefs and aquariums, and built the film around the only two things a father and son this damaged can actually say to each other. Albert Brooks is Marlin, who is frightened of everything; Ellen DeGeneres is Dory, who forgets everything, in the performance that revived her career; Alexander Gould is Nemo; and behind them Willem Dafoe, Brad Garrett, Allison Janney, Geoffrey Rush, Barry Humphries and John Ratzenberger fill in the tank gang, the pelican and the sharks. Thomas Newman's first Pixar score is the water itself. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature and was nominated for Best Original Screenplay - a category that almost never lets animation in. 100 minutes. If you only know it as the fish film, watch it again as the film about an overprotective man learning to let go, which is a thing you can only really appreciate once you have had to let go of something. IMDb 8.2.
